justification: The differentiation claim holds up: both ranking-style pages I could reach (GeeksforGeeks, Wikipedia) are static definitions or bullet/table comparisons with no worked example, no Gantt output and no code, while this article runs five real, verified C# implementations against one identical five-process workload, prints real Gantt traces and metrics, and states honestly where each algorithm loses as well as wins (MLFQ gets the best response time, 4.0, but the worst turnaround among the non-RR algorithms, 13.6 -- confirmed by re-reading the printed averages: FCFS 12.2/7.8/7.8, SJF 9.6/5.2/5.2, RR 13.8/9.4/5.4, Priority 11.4/7.0/7.0, MLFQ 13.6/9.2/4.0, and the prose explicitly says MLFQ's turnaround is 'worse than plain FCFS'). No close paraphrasing found against either comparator on spot-checked distinctive sentences. run-code.mjs passes clean (blocks=20, executed=10). No filler, no ad code; the toolchain sentence ('.NET 10.0.401 on Windows 11, x64') is correctly placed at the first measurement, not as an opening stamp. Headings are specific to content and structurally distinct from the only current sibling, processes-and-threads.md (which is organized around a sequence of demonstrations -- shared write, ownership diagram, crash, context-switch cost, creation cost, pool starvation -- versus this article's one-workload-per-algorithm shape); no other operating-systems siblings exist yet to compare against. The sched(7)-is-stale contrast is genuinely useful pedagogy, not a gimmick: it is tied to a real, verified fact (the man page still says CFS is the default; the kernel's own EEVDF doc says the kernel moved to EEVDF in 6.6) and used to make an explicit, transferable point about checking primary-source currency, not just a throwaway dig. Exercises cover predict/verify (SJF-vs-FCFS arithmetic), a second predict/verify (quantum shrink/grow), one true extend-the-code (implement aging), and one find-the-bug (single-admission RR loop); none of the predict-style exercises show their output before the solution. I independently verified 7 of the 9 cited claims against the live pages: the MS Learn 32-level range, the exact base-priority table values (NORMAL/NORMAL=8, HIGH/NORMAL=13), the priority-boost decay-by-one-per-slice quote, the 0-15 boost-eligibility cutoff, the CFS vruntime/red-black-tree/leftmost-task description, the sched(7) 'the default scheduler is CFS' quote, the nice value -20/+19 range, and (via the actual OSTEP PDFs, extracted with pdftotext since the fetch tool could not read them directly) the turnaround/response-time formulas, the convoy-effect citation, and the MLFQ Rules 1-5 including the old Rule 4a/4b gaming exploit -- all accurate. Two problems keep this out of pass range. First, and most serious: the sentence 'The kernel's own current scheduler documentation states it directly: CFS "is making room for EEVDF"' presents a direct quotation with citation, but the live EEVDF Scheduler page (docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html, fetched and also downloaded and grepped in full) does not contain that phrase anywhere; the actual sentence is 'moving away from the earlier Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) in favor of a version of EEVDF proposed by Peter Zijlstra in 2023.' The underlying fact (EEVDF replaced CFS as of 6.6) is correct, but the quoted words are invented, which is exactly what the brief's binding rule 'never fabricate ... quotes' forbids. Second, two of the nine listed sources are never cited inline anywhere in the body: 'Operating System Concepts, 10th ed., chapter 5: CPU Scheduling' and the base 'Scheduling (Win32 apps)' overview page (distinct from the Scheduling Priorities and Priority Boosts pages, which are both cited repeatedly) -- checked by grepping every markdown link in the article against the front-matter source list. The brief's binding pilot-round lesson treats an uncited listed source as a finding in its own right. Both are quick, concrete fixes, but a fabricated quotation is a hard-rule violation, not a style nit, so this cannot pass at round 1.

issues.location: "What Linux actually schedules, and why the textbook answer is dated", paragraph beginning "Linux 6.6, released in 2023, replaced CFS..."
issues.problem: Fabricated direct quotation. The sentence attributes the exact words 'is making room for EEVDF' to the cited kernel documentation page (docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html) with quotation marks and a citation link. I fetched the live page twice (once via a semantic re-read, once by downloading the raw HTML and grepping the full extracted body text for 'making room' and for 'room') and the phrase does not appear anywhere on the page. The page's actual sentence is: 'The Linux kernel began transitioning to EEVDF in version 6.6 (as a new option in 2024), moving away from the earlier Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) in favor of a version of EEVDF proposed by Peter Zijlstra in 2023.' The underlying claim (EEVDF replaced CFS starting in 6.6) is true and is otherwise accurately supported elsewhere in the same paragraph (the lag/virtual-deadline description matches the page closely), but presenting invented wording as a verbatim quote from a real, named, linked source is exactly the fabrication the brief's rules forbid, and it sits in the section built around the article's own 'check source currency' argument, which undercuts that argument's credibility.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace the quoted fragment with either a real quote from the page (e.g. '"moving away from the earlier Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) in favor of a version of EEVDF"') or drop the quotation marks and state it as a paraphrase in the article's own words, e.g. 'The kernel's own current scheduler documentation confirms the kernel moved away from CFS in favor of EEVDF starting in 6.6.'

issues.location: Front matter sources (lines 12-48) versus body: "Operating System Concepts, 10th ed., chapter 5: CPU Scheduling" (os-book.com/OS10/) and "Scheduling" (learn.microsoft.com/.../procthread/scheduling)
issues.problem: Two of the nine listed sources are never cited or linked anywhere in the article body. I grepped every markdown link in the file against the nine front-matter URLs: OSTEP ch.7 and ch.8, Scheduling Priorities, Priority Boosts, EEVDF, CFS design and sched(7) are all cited (several repeatedly), but os-book.com/OS10/ and the base procthread/scheduling overview page never appear as inline links or attributed claims. The brief's binding pilot-round lesson treats an uncited listed source as a finding: it reads as bibliography padding to a reviewer checking sourcing, and for a widely available textbook like Operating System Concepts it is also odd that a chapter is listed as a source and never drawn on for any claim the OSTEP citations don't already cover.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite Operating System Concepts ch.5 inline for a claim OSTEP does not already carry (for example the goals list, or the definition of a scheduling algorithm as a policy), and cite the base Scheduling overview page inline where the Windows section first states that threads (not processes) are scheduled, or remove both from the source list if the claims they'd support are already fully covered by the sources actually cited.

issues.location: "Shortest job first..." section, sentence "A preemptive variant... OSTEP proves SJF is optimal for average turnaround when all jobs arrive together, and STCF for the general case..."
issues.problem: Overstates the cited source for the SJF half of the claim. I read the OSTEP ch.7 PDF directly (pdftotext extraction): the book says 'we could prove that SJF is indeed an optimal scheduling algorithm. However, you are in a systems class, not theory or operations research; no proofs are allowed' -- i.e. OSTEP explicitly declines to prove SJF optimality, only asserting it. It does call STCF 'provably optimal' later, so the STCF half of the sentence is accurate as written, but 'OSTEP proves SJF is optimal' is not what the source does.
issues.fixLooksLike: Split the claim: 'OSTEP asserts (without a formal proof, by its own admission) that SJF is optimal for average turnaround when all jobs arrive together, and states STCF is provably optimal for the general case...' or similar.

issues.location: Exercises: "Do the arithmetic before you run it" (SJF/FCFS) and "Shrink and grow the quantum" (RR)
issues.problem: Of the four exercises, two share the same shape (predict a numeric outcome from given inputs, then run a program the solution supplies to confirm it), leaving one true extend-the-code exercise (aging) and one find-the-bug exercise. This satisfies the brief's literal 'vary the form' rule (three distinct forms appear across four exercises) and neither predict exercise leaks its output before the solution, so it is not a rule violation, but it is less variety than the four canonical forms (predict / extend / find-the-bug / prove-it or measure-it) would give, and a reviewer comparing this article's exercise section end to end will notice the repeated predict-then-verify shape.
